paragraphs.heading: What Mir was
paragraphs.text: Mir, a Russian word meaning 'peace' or 'world', was a space station that circled Earth in low orbit from 1986 to 2001. The Soviet Union ran it first, and Russia took over later. It was the first modular space station, put together in orbit piece by piece between 1986 and 1996. In its day it was the largest artificial satellite in orbit, and the ISS took that title only after Mir was brought down in 2001.

paragraphs.heading: A lab for living in space
paragraphs.text: Mir served as a research lab in microgravity. Crews ran experiments in physics, astronomy, meteorology, biology, human biology and spacecraft systems, aiming at the technology people would need to live in space for good. It was the first long-term research station in orbit to be lived in without a break, and it held the record for continuous human presence, 3,644 days, until the ISS passed it in 2010. Valeri Polyakov spent 437 days aboard in 1994 and 1995, still the longest single human spaceflight. In all, 105 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations visited and made 80 spacewalks.

paragraphs.heading: Built from modules
paragraphs.text: Mir came after six crewed Salyut stations, each made of a single module. It ended up with seven pressurised modules and several unpressurised parts, starting with the Core Module in 1986. Proton rockets launched every piece except the Docking Module, which the Space Shuttle installed on mission STS-74. Solar panels fixed straight onto the modules supplied power. The station orbited 296 to 421 km up, at an inclination of 51.6°, and circled Earth 15.7 times a day.

paragraphs.heading: How new modules arrived
paragraphs.text: New modules followed a set routine. Each one flew up alone on a Proton-K rocket and met the station automatically. It docked first at the forward docking node of the core module, then used its own Lyappa arm to grip a fixture, swing itself to another port and dock there. The node had only two Konus drogues, fittings that dockings needed, so before each new module came, the node was depressurised and spacewalking cosmonauts moved a drogue by hand to the next port. Two modules, Kvant-1 and the Docking Module, were exceptions.

paragraphs.heading: Kvant-1, the exception
paragraphs.text: Kvant-1 had first been designed for the Salyut 7 station and had no propulsion system of its own. A space tug based on the TKS spacecraft carried it instead, bringing it to the rear docking node of the core module rather than the front one. Kvant-1 docked on 11 April 1987, and the next day the tug disposed of itself.

paragraphs.heading: A race to launch
paragraphs.text: In early 1984 work on Mir stopped while resources went to the Buran programme. It restarted when Valentin Glushko was ordered to have Mir in orbit by early 1986, ahead of the 27th Congress of the Communist Party. The normal processing steps could not meet that date, so on 12 April 1985 the decision was made to send the base block's flight model to the Baikonur Cosmodrome and test it there. A first launch try on 16 February 1986 was called off when communications failed, but the second, on 19 February, worked and met the political deadline.

paragraphs.heading: Visitors, cost and end
paragraphs.text: Most people aboard were Soviet or Russian, but programmes such as Interkosmos, Euromir and Shuttle–Mir opened the station to travellers from several nations in Asia, Europe and North America. After its funding was cut off, Mir was brought down from orbit in March 2001. Yuri Koptev, a former head of the Russian space agency, put the cost of the whole programme at $4.2 billion. As of 2026, Mir was the setting for half of the ten longest human spaceflights.
